title: RBI Could Raise Repo Rate by 75–100 bps This Cycle, SBI Capital Says
excerpt: SBI Capital Markets expects the repo rate to climb further from 5.5% as inflation persists, with a possible larger hike at the December MPC review depending on September and October price data.
body:
• SBI Capital Markets expects the RBI to lift the repo rate by 75–100 basis points over the current tightening cycle — up from 5.50% after the October 7 hike, the first increase in nearly four years.
  • The brokerage's base case is gradual hikes, but a larger-than-usual move at the December MPC review is on the table, contingent on September and October inflation prints.
  • CPI inflation rose to 4.8% in August and is expected to peak in Q3 FY27; the RBI has raised its FY27 inflation forecast to 5.2% while upgrading GDP growth to 7.1%.
  • Borrower watch: floating-rate home and auto loans will get costlier as banks pass through the hikes — review prepayment options or a switch to fixed rates; savers, meanwhile, should see fixed-deposit rates climb as bond yields stay elevated.

The Reserve Bank of India has only just begun raising rates — and it may have a long way to go. In a report published Friday, SBI Capital Markets said the RBI could lift the repo rate by 75–100 basis points during the current tightening cycle, as inflationary pressures are expected to persist before easing in the next financial year.

The call lands three days after the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% on October 7 — its first hike since February 2023 — and shifted its stance from "Neutral" to "Calibrated Tightening." That shift, SBI Capital said, signals a stronger emphasis on containing inflation. Governor Sanjay Malhotra has made clear that rate cuts are off the table for now: future policy action, he said, "can only be a rate hike or a pause."

Context & Background

The SBI Capital report expects consumer price inflation to peak in the third quarter of FY27, while wholesale price inflation could begin moderating from March 2027 as favourable base effects set in. Retail inflation is expected to remain below 5% year-on-year only beyond the first quarter of FY28 — the point at which the brokerage sees the policy cycle reversing.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=lWJGSIZEFPo

The backdrop is a central bank caught between resilient growth and broadening price pressures. Retail inflation climbed to 4.8% in August from 4.5% in July, with core inflation at 4.2%, and the RBI raised its FY27 CPI forecast to 5.2% from 5%. At the same time, India's economy expanded 7.8% in the June quarter, beating expectations of 7.1%, prompting the RBI to upgrade its full-year growth forecast to 7.1% from 6.7%. Manufacturing grew 9.2% and gross fixed capital formation rose 11.9%.

"With FY27 GDP growth estimated at 7.1%, the economy has room to absorb tighter policy, and the RBI is right to act as inflation becomes increasingly broad-based."

— Maulik Patel, Head of Research, Equirus Securities

But the report flagged risks to consumption in the second half of FY27: rising borrowing costs, subdued rural sentiment and weaker kharif sowing could weigh on demand, while crude oil around $100 a barrel and prolonged geopolitical conflicts keep cost pressures alive. Benchmark 10-year government bond yields have risen about 70 basis points in calendar 2026, and SBI Capital expects them to stay elevated until geopolitical tensions ease.

Impact & Analysis

For borrowers, the direction of travel is clear: EMIs on floating-rate home, vehicle and business loans linked to the repo rate are set to rise further as banks pass through each hike. Borrowers with long tenors may want to consider prepayments or locking into fixed rates before the next moves. Savers get the mirror image — deposit rates are likely to harden as lenders compete for funds, and the report expects bonds to regain investor interest in FY28 as inflation eases and the cycle turns.

Banks themselves stand to benefit in the near term. Higher rates are expected to support bank margins, SBI Capital said, although non-food credit growth could gradually lose momentum toward the end of FY27. The brokerage expects FY27 to remain favourable for the banking sector overall.

The report cautioned that rising yields in advanced economies and capital outflows from emerging markets are adding to uncertainty, with the rupee's weakness and elevated oil prices the key external variables to watch.

The diaspora angle is direct: NRIs holding home loans in India face higher EMIs on floating-rate debt, while those keeping surplus savings in NRE or NRO fixed deposits should see improving rates as the tightening cycle runs its course.

What's Next

All eyes are on the next MPC review in December 2026. SBI Capital's base case is a gradual sequence of increases, but it said a larger hike in December cannot be ruled out — the call will hinge on September and October inflation readings. Beyond that, the brokerage expects the cycle to begin reversing in the first quarter of FY28, depending on how the growth-inflation balance evolves.
